title: Two neutron stars merging
what: GW170817, the first wave in space heard from two neutron stars, on 17 August 2017, and the first also seen in light: told as a story of its source, two neutron stars spiralling together and merging 130 million light-years away; what its wave does to space as it passes, a ring of free masses stretched and squeezed; how LIGO Livingston heard it; and the kilonova it lit, with the heavy elements, gold and platinum among them, that were detected, inferred or expected.
how: The wave is a model, not LIGO’s measured waveform: a Newtonian chirp for the chirp mass the detectors measured, 1.1977 Suns (1.188 at the source, its light stretched by its distance), seen face on from 40 Mpc. Two neutron stars are light and, until their last orbits, far apart for their size, so this simple model follows the true wave closely until they touch; its strain, about 5 × 10⁻²² at the end, is worked out from that formula, h = 4(G𝓜/c²)^⁵ᐟ³(πf/c)^²ᐟ³/D, not measured. The detectors heard the wave from 24 Hz for about 100 s, some 3,000 cycles; played here is its last fifth of a second, from 250 Hz to about 1.5 kHz, where two stars 11.9 km in radius touch. Nothing after the merger was heard: a black hole’s ringing would be near 6 kHz, beyond the detectors’ reach, and searches found no signal from a remnant. So the wave stops at the merger. It is drawn as GW150914 is, at the same stretch, 4 × 10²⁰, and slowed 100 times: it sways about half as much, ten times nearer but from stars some twenty-five times lighter. The source is drawn from above its orbit: the two stars at their masses’ ratio, 1.46 and 1.27 Suns (GWTC-1’s medians), going round at half the wave’s frequency, closing in as the pitch rises by Kepler’s third law, a³ = GM/ω². Their size is drawn true against their distance apart (11.9 km against 84 km when the wave is first played, 25 km when they touch), not against the sheet. As they close in, each is drawn pulled out of round toward the other, by an amount that grows as (R/a)³, the tide’s strength: that the tides shaped the wave is measured (it is how the radius was found); the shape drawn is not. What they made is drawn as one hot, glowing body, half again as wide: not measured. The sheet and its spiral are worked out as for GW150914. “Hear it” plays the chirp slowed 10 times at its own pitch, which, unlike GW150914’s, falls in the range we hear. The kilonova chapter draws what was flung out as Kasen et al. (2017) read it from the light of AT 2017gfo: a fast component, about 0.025 Suns at 0.3c, as points streaming out within 45° of the orbit’s poles, and a slow one, about 0.04 Suns at 0.1c, as points within 35° of the orbit’s plane; each point is placed by its speed, more slow than fast. That geometry follows their picture (polar ejecta squeezed out as the stars touch, a wind from the disk about the remnant), not a measured map. The ejecta expand keeping their shape, so the cloud is drawn at one size and the clock gives the fast edge’s true distance, 0.3c times the time since the merger (about 52 AU a day). Each glows by a simple model (Metzger 2020): heated by its radioactive nuclei at ė ≈ 2 × 10¹⁰ ε (t/day)^−1.3 erg/s/g, with half the heat (ε) kept, it shines with all of it once light can diffuse out, from about t_peak = 1.6 d (M/0.01 M☉)^½ (v/0.1c)^−½ (κ/1 cm²/g)^½, and with the share (t/t_peak)^3/2 of it before. With an opacity of 0.5 cm²/g the blue peaks after about a day; with 10, as lanthanides make it, the red after about ten. Each is drawn against its own peak. The clock runs from an hour to four weeks on a log scale, and names what was seen when: found by the Swope telescope 10.9 hours after, strontium in its spectrum at 1.5 days, the blue fading within two, X-rays at about 9 days and radio at about 16. “Gold and platinum” gives what was detected (strontium), inferred (the lanthanides, and gold as worked out on the Sun’s pattern), not seen (gold and platinum lines), and expected (the r-process’s three peaks), each with its paper.
certainty: Stretched 4 × 10²⁰ times and slowed 100 times, to be seen: over LIGO’s 4 km arms the real change, at its largest, was about 2 × 10⁻¹⁸ m, under a thousandth of a proton’s width.

The wave played is a Newtonian model fitted to the measured chirp mass, not the measured strain: in the last few orbits, where tides and the stars’ own fields matter most, the true wave runs a little ahead of it.

The masses are ranges: 1.36 to 1.60 and 1.17 to 1.36 Suns if the stars spun slowly, as known neutron-star pairs do, and 0.86 to 2.26 if they may have spun fast. The radius, 11.9 ± 1.4 km, assumes both stars are made of the same matter and that neutron stars can reach about two Suns.
The stars’ shapes as they are pulled, the glow drawn about them, and the size of what they made are drawn to show what happens, not measured.

The kilonova’s light is a one-zone model with two components, not the measured light curve; its masses, speeds and opacities are approximate, as Kasen et al. say, and the gold is worked out from them on an assumed pattern, not measured: no line of gold or platinum was seen.
others: What the merger made is not settled. Its mass, about 2.7 Suns, is more than a neutron star is thought to hold for long, so most readings have it collapse into a black hole, within a second or so, after a brief life as a hot, spinning, overweight neutron star; others allow a neutron star that lived longer. The gravitational waves cannot tell: nothing after the merger was heard. Where most gold is made is disputed too: Kasen et al. (2017) find mergers like this could make all of it if they are common enough and fling out 0.01 Suns or more; Siegel et al. (2019) find collapsars, the collapse of fast-spinning massive stars, may make more than 80% of these elements.
